## Overview

This gallery shows every plotting function of NanoQuRe on the dataset bundled
with the package, first with its default settings and then with the arguments
that change the picture. Each plot is followed by a short note on how it may
be read and on what it cannot show. All plots are interactive: hovering over
a trace displays the underlying values, and the legend toggles individual
traces.

## Example data

Two datasets are used. The bundled `sample_data` object holds 1000 reads of a
single MinION run and serves the read length and Q-score distributions. Its
reads come from the first minutes and the last half hour of the run only, so
it cannot illustrate the plots that follow a run over time.

```{r load-data}
library(NanoQuRe)

data(sample_data)
```

The time-resolved plots therefore use a simulated run, generated below:
200,000 reads on 512 channels over 48 h, in which channels stop producing
reads at different times and both the translocation speed and the Q-score
decline slowly. These data are artificial. They only illustrate what the
plots look like for a complete run and carry no biological meaning.

```{r simulate-run}
set.seed(123) # reproducible simulation

n_reads <- 200000
n_channels <- 512
run_seconds <- 48 * 3600

# each channel stops producing reads at its own time
channel_end <- pmin(stats::rweibull(n_channels, shape = 1.5, scale = 30) * 3600,
                    run_seconds)
# channels that live longer contribute more reads
channel <- sample(seq_len(n_channels), n_reads, replace = TRUE, prob = channel_end)
start_time <- stats::runif(n_reads, min = 0, max = channel_end[channel])
run_fraction <- start_time / run_seconds

# log-normal read lengths; speed and quality decline over the run
read_length <- round(stats::rlnorm(n_reads, meanlog = 6.8, sdlog = .9)) + 20
speed <- stats::rnorm(n_reads, mean = 400 - 60 * run_fraction, sd = 25)
qscore <- stats::rnorm(n_reads, mean = 12.5 - 2 * run_fraction, sd = 2)

simulated_run <- data.frame(
  sample_id = "simulated_run",
  run_id = "simulated_run_1",
  channel = channel,
  start_time = start_time,
  duration = read_length / pmax(speed, 50),
  sequence_length_template = read_length,
  mean_qscore_template = qscore,
  # pass/fail threshold of the simulated basecaller
  passes_filtering = qscore >= 9
)
```

Every function returns an ordinary plotly object (`plot_double()` returns a
named list of two), which can be modified with plotly functions or embedded
in an R Markdown document. The summary tables and `generate_report()` are
described in the [Getting Started](getting-started.html) and
[Using Individual Functions](individual-functions.html) vignettes.

## Read length and quality

### `plot_read_lengths()`

The plot shows a histogram of read lengths drawn as a step line, with sequence
length in nt on the x axis (logarithmic by default) and the number of reads per
bin on the y axis. Vertical lines mark the mean read length and the N50.

```{r lq-read-lengths-default}
plot_read_lengths(sample_data)
```

With `weight = "bases"`, each bin is scaled by the number of bases it contains
instead of the number of reads, which shifts the visual weight towards long
reads.

```{r lq-read-lengths-bases}
plot_read_lengths(sample_data, weight = "bases")
```

A linear axis combined with `upper_limit` truncates the view; reads beyond the
limit are counted in a note at the top right of the plot.

```{r lq-read-lengths-linear}
plot_read_lengths(sample_data, log_x = FALSE, upper_limit = 5000)
```

Because the result is an ordinary plotly object, it can be modified further
with plotly functions.

```{r lq-read-lengths-custom}
length_plot <- plot_read_lengths(sample_data)
plotly::layout(length_plot, title = list(text = "Read lengths, MinION run"))
```

**Reading the plot.** In `sample_data` the mean read length is 1083 nt, the
median is 712 nt, and the N50 is 1201 nt; the mean and N50 lie well to the
right of the bulk of the reads because a few very long reads (the longest is
43360 nt; 10 reads exceed 10000 nt) pull both upwards. The base-weighted view
shows the same effect: reads longer than 10000 nt are 1% of reads but carry
about 24% of the bases. The plot describes length only; it says nothing about
the quality of those reads or about when in the run they were produced.

### `plot_quality_distribution()`

The plot shows a stacked histogram of the mean Q-score of each read (x axis)
against the number of reads (y axis), with fail reads and pass reads in
separate colours. A dashed vertical line marks the user-defined cut-off
(`qscore_cutoff`), and a solid line marks the lowest Q-score among pass reads,
which approximates the basecaller threshold.

```{r lq-quality-default}
plot_quality_distribution(sample_data)
```

Raising `qscore_cutoff` moves the dashed line, which is useful for judging how
many reads would remain under a stricter custom filter.

```{r lq-quality-cutoff}
plot_quality_distribution(sample_data, qscore_cutoff = 10)
```

**Reading the plot.** In `sample_data` 885 reads pass and 115 fail; the
basecaller threshold is at about Q8.01, so the default cut-off of Q7 lies below
it and 61 fail reads sit above that line. The median read Q-score is 11.29, and
300 reads fall below Q10. The histogram describes per-read means only; it
cannot show how quality varies within a read, nor why a given read failed.

### `plot_double()`

The function returns a named list of two plots that share the same x axis, time
since the start of the run in hours. `length_plot` shows the maximum, average,
and minimum read length per hour on a logarithmic y axis, and `qscore_plot`
shows the maximum, average, and minimum mean Q-score per hour. Because
`sample_data` covers only two short periods of a run, the plots below use the
simulated run described above.

```{r lq-double-length}
double_plots <- plot_double(simulated_run)
double_plots$length_plot
```

```{r lq-double-qscore}
double_plots$qscore_plot
```

**Reading the plot.** These data are simulated and only illustrate the plot.
The average Q-score falls from 12.47 in the first hour to 11.48 in hour 23 and
10.50 in hour 47, a slow decline of the kind that may indicate pore or flow
cell ageing in a real run. The average read length stays near 1350 nt
throughout, whereas the maximum varies widely from hour to hour (27660 nt in
the first hour, 15709 nt in the last), because it is determined by single
reads and is sensitive to the number of reads in each hour. The plots show
per-hour extremes and means only, so they cannot reveal how many reads
contribute to each hour or which channels are responsible for a change.

## Yield, throughput, and speed

### `plot_cumulative_yield()`

The plot shows the cumulative number of sequenced bases (in Gb, y axis) against
the start time of the reads (in hours, x axis), with one trace for pass reads
and one for fail reads. Reads are sorted by start time and summed in order; the
value at each time bin is the running total at its last read, and `max_points`
caps the number of bins per trace (a bin is never narrower than one minute).
The examples in this section use the simulated run, so the numbers illustrate
the plots and carry no biological meaning.

```{r ys-cumulative-default}
plot_cumulative_yield(simulated_run)
```

Restricting the input to the first 12 h of the run, with a small `max_points`,
gives a coarser trace over a shorter time axis.

```{r ys-cumulative-first12}
first_12h <- simulated_run[simulated_run$start_time < 12 * 3600, ]
plot_cumulative_yield(first_12h, max_points = 50L)
```

The returned object is an ordinary plotly object, so it can be modified with
plotly functions, for example to change the title and the x axis range.

```{r ys-cumulative-layout}
yield_plot <- plot_cumulative_yield(simulated_run)
plotly::layout(
  yield_plot,
  title = list(text = "Cumulative yield, first 24 h"),
  xaxis = list(range = c(0, 24))
)
```

**Reading the plot.** The pass reads reach about 0.249 Gb and the fail reads
about 0.024 Gb (8.8% of reads fail) by the end of the 48 h. The slope of the
pass trace flattens over time, which suggests that fewer reads were started in
the later hours, in line with the channels in the simulation stopping one after
another. The plot cannot indicate why the slope changes, because a loss of
active pores, a loss of library, and a change in read length all lower it.

### `plot_seq_throughput()`

The plot shows the yield per hour (in Gb, y axis) against run time (in hours,
x axis), separately for pass and fail reads. Each read is assigned to the hour
in which it started, the read lengths of each hour are summed, and every hour
between the first and the last read is included, with hours without reads set
to zero.

```{r ys-throughput-default}
plot_seq_throughput(simulated_run)
```

The same plot for the first 12 h of the run, which shows the early hours at a
finer scale.

```{r ys-throughput-first12}
plot_seq_throughput(first_12h)
```

**Reading the plot.** The pass throughput is highest in the first hour (about
0.0103 Gb) and falls to about 0.0050 Gb in hour 23 and about 0.0009 Gb in hour
47, whereas the fail throughput stays between about 0.0003 and 0.0006 Gb per
hour. A decline of this kind may reflect pores becoming inactive, but the plot
does not show which channels stopped. Hours without reads appear as zero yield
and cannot be told apart from an interruption of the run, and a long read is
counted wholly in the hour in which it started.

### `plot_average_speed()`

The plot shows the mean translocation speed (in nt/s, y axis) per hour of run
time (x axis) for pass and fail reads. The speed of an hour is the summed read
length divided by the summed read duration of the reads that started in that
hour, which weights long reads more heavily than a mean of per-read speeds.

```{r ys-speed-default}
plot_average_speed(simulated_run)
```

The same plot for pass reads only, which removes the noisier fail trace and
makes the trend of the pass reads easier to follow.

```{r ys-speed-pass}
pass_reads <- simulated_run[simulated_run$passes_filtering, ]
plot_average_speed(pass_reads)
```

**Reading the plot.** The pass speed declines from about 398 nt/s in hour 0 to
about 384 nt/s in hour 11, about 370 nt/s in hour 23, and about 339 nt/s in
hour 47, and the fail reads follow almost the same course. A slow decline of
this kind is commonly attributed to ageing of the flow cell or depletion of
reagents, although the plot alone cannot confirm a cause. The speed is derived
from the `duration` field of the sequencing summary and is not a direct
measurement of motor kinetics, and hours without reads would appear as gaps in
the line.

## Channel activity

The plots of this group use the simulated run (`simulated_run`) described above;
the data are artificial and only illustrate the plots.

### `plot_active_channels()`

The plot shows the number of channels with at least one read overlapping each
time window. Dashed lines mark the first window in which the count falls to the
given fractions (`thresholds`) of the highest count in the first hour; the final
window, which is usually partial, is not searched.

```{r ch-active-default}
plot_active_channels(simulated_run)
```

A wider window (one hour instead of ten minutes) smooths the short-term
fluctuations of the count.

```{r ch-active-wide}
plot_active_channels(simulated_run, bin_width = 1)
```

Other fractions of the first-hour maximum can be marked with `thresholds`.

```{r ch-active-thresholds}
plot_active_channels(simulated_run, thresholds = c(.75, .5, .25))
```

A threshold that is never reached is reported in a note on the plot instead of
a dashed line; here 5% of the first-hour maximum is not reached.

```{r ch-active-unreached}
plot_active_channels(simulated_run, thresholds = c(.5, .25, .05),
                     bin_width = 1)
```

**Reading the plot.** All 512 channels produced reads in `simulated_run`, and
the first-hour maximum is 479 active channels with the default window (512 with
`bin_width = 1`). With the default window, the count falls to 50% of that
maximum at 24.5 h and to 25% at 36.5 h; the final window still holds 55
active channels (about 11%) and, with one-hour windows, the last window holds
63 (about 12%), which is why the 5% line is absent. A channel
without reads in a window is not necessarily exhausted, and pore scans and
pauses are not recorded in the sequencing summary, so a decline of the count
may reflect several processes that these data cannot separate.

### `pore_activity_heatmap()`

The figure has two panels: the upper one shows bases per channel per time bin
(channels on the x axis, run time on the y axis), and the lower one shows bases
per channel arranged according to the physical layout of the flow cell.

```{r ch-heatmap-default}
pore_activity_heatmap(simulated_run)
```

A coarser time bin reduces the number of rows of the upper panel.

```{r ch-heatmap-coarse}
pore_activity_heatmap(simulated_run, bin_width = 6)
```

The PromethION layout is illustrated with a second, small simulated summary
(3000 reads on channels 1 to 3000, one `run_id`, 24 h) that only illustrates the
3000-channel layout.

```{r ch-heatmap-promethion}
set.seed(123) # reproducible simulation
n_prom <- 3000
prom_summary <- data.frame(
  run_id = "simulated_promethion_1",
  sample_id = "simulated_promethion",
  channel = sample(seq_len(3000), n_prom, replace = TRUE),
  start_time = stats::runif(n_prom, min = 0, max = 24 * 3600),
  duration = stats::rlnorm(n_prom, meanlog = 1, sdlog = .7),
  sequence_length_template = round(stats::rlnorm(n_prom, meanlog = 7.5,
                                                 sdlog = .8)),
  mean_qscore_template = stats::rnorm(n_prom, mean = 11, sd = 2)
)
prom_summary$passes_filtering <- prom_summary$mean_qscore_template >= 9

pore_activity_heatmap(prom_summary, platform = "promethion", bin_width = 2)
```

**Reading the plot.** In `simulated_run`, the 100 channels with the most bases
account for about 36% of the 273 million bases and the 100 channels with the
fewest for about 5%, so the yield per channel is uneven. Dark cells in the upper
panel show when and on which channels the bases were produced; the lower panel
shows whether high and low yields cluster in regions of the flow cell. The
summary data do not identify the physical cause of differences between channels
or regions. The function requires a single `run_id`, and channel numbers outside
the selected layout (1 to 512 for MinION, 1 to 3000 for PromethION) stop it
with an error, so `platform` has to match the data. Flongle flow cells are not
supported.
